selected_result: Langlois–Louvet Theorem 4 and equation (13): absolute forward-error bound for compensated Horner evaluation

bibliographic_source.title: Faithful Polynomial Evaluation with Compensated Horner Algorithm

paper_locations.anchor: IEEE-754 working precision, round-to-nearest, normalized floating coefficients and input, no overflow or underflow
EFTHorner obtains the ordinary Horner value and two exact-error polynomials using TwoProd and TwoSum
CompHorner evaluates the coefficientwise rounded sum of the two error polynomials by Horner, then adds the correction to the original result
|CompHorner(p,x)-p(x)| ≤ u|p(x)|+gamma_(2n)^2 times the absolute-coefficient polynomial at |x|

task_clarification: For every degree n polynomial p with floating-point coefficients and floating-point argument x, compute the complete EFTHorner and CompHorner algorithms of Algorithms 5–6, including TwoProd/TwoSum residuals, the coefficientwise rounded p_pi+p_sigma, its ordinary Horner evaluation, and the final rounded correction.
Under the source's no-overflow/no-underflow and gamma-valid arithmetic conditions, formalize |CompHorner(p,x)-p(x)| ≤ u*|p(x)|+gamma_(2*n)^2*tilde_p(x), where tilde_p(x)=sum_i |a_i|*|x|^i.
The target is the full forward-error inequality, not merely a statement about ordinary Horner, EFTHorner's exact decomposition, or an assumed abstract correction-error bound.
scope_constraints: Retain all polynomial degrees and all floating coefficients and inputs in the source domain; do not narrow to positive coefficients, sign-stable evaluations, or a fixed degree.
Preserve the complete Algorithm 6 and the squared gamma_(2n) factor and non-strict inequality.
Do not assume the target bound in a model/interface hypothesis. A task-local EFT implementation is permitted, with only source-equivalent arithmetic laws.
The source globally assumes no underflow or overflow; do not silently drop these or add a stronger semantic restriction.
The source text writes the result for degree n, while Algorithm 5 forms degree n-1 residual polynomials; handle the n=0 endpoint explicitly and faithfully rather than making it vacuous.
